n: The great turn in Solomon’s story begins with one word: “But.” He loved many foreign women, many from nations whose worship Israel was warned against. These marriages were also political alliances.

f.g: foreign women, from outside Israel’s covenant.
people of Sidon, a Phoenician city.

n: The Lord had forbidden intermarriage with these nations precisely because it would draw Israel’s hearts toward other gods. Solomon “clave” to them—held on tightly in love—despite the warning.

f.w: Ye shall not go in to them

f.g: clung, held fast.

n: The numbers are enormous: seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines. The Book of Mormon calls this an abomination, and the D&C explains that Solomon sinned in the wives he took without the Lord’s sanction.

f.g: secondary wives with lower legal status.

n: As he aged, his heart drifted. It was “not perfect”—not whole or undivided—toward the Lord as David’s had been. The danger was gradual, not sudden.

f.g: Hebrew shalem: whole, complete, at peace; related to ‘Solomon’ (Shelomoh).

n: Solomon followed Ashtoreth (Astarte), the Phoenician fertility goddess, and Milcom, the national god of Ammon.

f.g: Astarte, Canaanite and Phoenician goddess of fertility and war.
something detestable to God, often a name for an idol.

n: The verdict: Solomon did evil. He did not follow the Lord “fully,” as David had, meaning his loyalty was divided.
He built shrines for Chemosh of Moab and Molech of Ammon on the Mount of Olives, facing the temple itself. Molech worship could involve child sacrifice.

f.g: national god of Moab.
Ammonite god associated with child sacrifice.

f.w: the hill that is before Jerusalem
f.g: the Mount of Olives, east of the temple.

n: He provided places of worship for the gods of each foreign wife. What began as tolerance became sponsorship of idolatry.
The Lord’s anger is sharpened by the fact that He had personally appeared to Solomon twice. Greater light brings greater accountability.
Solomon had been specifically warned against this very thing, yet he did not obey.

f.w: that he should not go after other gods

n: The Lord announces judgment: the kingdom will be torn away and given to one of Solomon’s servants.

f.g: tear, rip apart.

n: Out of loyalty to David, the Lord will delay the division until after Solomon’s death.
Even in judgment there is mercy: one tribe (Judah, with Benjamin closely joined) will remain with David’s line for the sake of the covenant and Jerusalem.

f.g: Judah; Benjamin also stayed with Judah (1 Kings 12:21).

n: Trouble begins on the borders. Hadad, an Edomite prince, becomes the first adversary the Lord allows to rise against Solomon.

f.g: Hebrew satan: an opponent or adversary.

n: Background: years earlier, David’s general Joab had led a brutal campaign in Edom.
Joab stayed six months, trying to wipe out Edom’s males.
Hadad, then only a boy, escaped with some of his father’s officials and fled toward Egypt.
The refugees traveled through Midian and the wilderness of Paran, gathered men, and reached Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, food, and land—keeping a potential ally against Israel.

f.g: food supplies.
the wilderness region of the Sinai peninsula.

n: Hadad was so favored that Pharaoh married him to the queen’s sister, tying him to the royal family.

f.g: an Egyptian queen’s name or title; otherwise unknown.

n: Hadad’s son Genubath was raised among Pharaoh’s own sons.
Once David and Joab were dead, Hadad asked to go home to Edom—clearly to reclaim his people’s independence.

f.g: died; a gentle idiom for death.

n: Pharaoh asks what he lacks. Hadad says nothing, but insists on leaving—his heart was set on Edom.

f.g: by all means, in any case.

n: A second adversary appears: Rezon, a former officer of Hadadezer, the Aramean king David had defeated.
Rezon led a band of raiders, seized Damascus, and made himself king there.

f.g: the capital of Aram (Syria), north of Israel.

n: Rezon hated Israel and troubled it throughout Solomon’s reign. His kingdom of Aram would become one of Israel’s chief enemies.

f.g: Hebrew Aram; the Aramean kingdom centered on Damascus.

n: The third and most important adversary arises from within: Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite official raised by a widowed mother.

f.g: here, an Ephraimite.
rebelled.

n: The story of his rebellion begins with Solomon’s building projects in Jerusalem, where Jeroboam worked.

f.g: gaps or broken places in the wall.

n: Seeing that he was capable and hardworking, Solomon put Jeroboam over the forced labor from the house of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh)—exactly the northern tribes who resented that labor.

f.g: the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.
burden; the work crews and their obligations.

n: The prophet Ahijah from Shiloh, the old site of the tabernacle, meets Jeroboam alone outside the city, wearing a new cloak.

f.g: from Shiloh, where the tabernacle once stood.

n: Ahijah tears his own new garment into twelve pieces—an acted-out prophecy, like a parable performed in real life.
The twelve pieces represent the twelve tribes. Jeroboam is to take ten, a sign that the Lord will give him ten tribes.
One tribe stays with David’s line, for the sake of David and the chosen city.
The reason is idolatry: the people, led by Solomon, worshiped the gods of Sidon, Moab, and Ammon instead of keeping the Lord’s commandments.

f.g: the Hebrew is plural; some ancient versions read ‘he has forsaken me.’

n: Solomon himself will remain king for life, again for David’s sake.
The division will come under Solomon’s son.
A “light” in Jerusalem means a living heir—David’s lamp would keep burning. Latter-day Saints see this preserved line as leading to the Messiah, the Son of David.

f.g: a lamp; a symbol of a continuing royal line.

n: The Lord offers Jeroboam the throne of Israel and the fulfillment of his ambitions.
This is an extraordinary promise: if Jeroboam obeys as David did, the Lord will build him a lasting dynasty too. The tragedy of the next chapters is that he does not.

f.g: an enduring dynasty.

n: David’s descendants will be humbled, “but not for ever”—a hint of eventual restoration under a future son of David.
Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who escapes to Shishak of Egypt. Shishak (Sheshonq I) would later invade Judah.

f.g: Pharaoh Sheshonq I, founder of Egypt’s 22nd dynasty.

n: The writer cites a source, the “book of the acts of Solomon,” now lost. Kings regularly points readers to such royal records.

f.w: the book of the acts of Solomon
f.g: a lost royal chronicle used as a source.

n: Solomon reigned forty years over a united Israel—a round number matching David’s reign.
Solomon dies and is buried in Jerusalem. His son Rehoboam inherits a kingdom on the edge of breaking apart.
